steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper presenting RGBGrasp, our method for object grasping from RGB images captured by an arm-mounted camera, using neural radiance fields. Cover the limits of point-cloud and existing RGB-based approaches and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Grasping needs accurate 3D geometry; point-cloud sensors fall short
- RGB-based grasping from a single image
- Multi-view RGB / NeRF-based grasping
- Remaining challenges of multi-view methods
- RGBGrasp: our approach
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Grasping and point clouds
  - pivotal challenge: diverse morphology and materials of real objects
  - needs accurate 3D geometry, esp. for grasp pose
  - point-cloud sensors common (cite) but fail on transparent/specular objects -> unreliable 3D info
  - low resolution, noise (cite)

- Single-image RGB
  - growing interest in RGB modality
  - one work: single RGB image -> 3D object detection + pose (cite)
  - another: single image -> 2D keypoints + depth (cite)

- Multi-view RGB
  - single image: no scale info, inherently hard (cite)
  - so most current approaches use multi-view RGB to reconstruct 3D scenes
  - one method uses NeRF (cite) (cite) to aggregate viewpoints -> precise grasping across materials

- Challenges
  - explicit geometry for transparent/specular objects still hard
  - unnatural multi-view capture, e.g. orbiting around the scene (cite); impractical for shelves, walls
  - long learning times

- RGBGrasp
  - multi-view grasping, high-resolution 3D target scenarios
  - eye-on-hand camera captures views as gripper approaches object; small disparities
  - goal: precise and fast reconstruction
  - monocular depth priors (pre-trained) + NeRF reconstruction for limited views
  - hash encoding + new sampling proposal network for speed

- Contributions
  - depth rank loss (cite) with trained depth estimator; sparse views; beats conventional NeRF with constrained angles
  - hash encoding + proposal sampler -> faster reconstruction
  - experiments: multi-view and sparse-view, grasping and perception; consistently better than recent approaches

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Robotic object grasping is a key challenge in robotics, because real-world objects have very diverse shapes and material properties. To do the task we need accurate estimation of the 3D geometry, especially for deciding the grasping pose afterwards. Point-cloud sensors are common in current approaches, but they have trouble with transparent and specular objects, so in these cases the 3D information about the environment that they capture is unreliable. Also, the point clouds from these sensors often have low resolution and suffer from problems like noise.

Because of these issues, there is growing interest in using the RGB modality to improve object grasping. One line of research tries to get 3D scene perception from a single image. For example, one work uses a single RGB image to estimate 3D object detection and pose, and another work uses a single image to predict 2D keypoints together with their depth information.

The reasoning behind single-image grasping models is simple, but inferring 3D geometry from just one image is inherently hard, mainly because there is no scale information. So current approaches mostly use multi-view RGB data to reconstruct the full 3D scene. For example, one method uses the neural radiance field (NeRF) framework to combine information from multiple viewpoints, and in this way gets precise grasping for objects with different material properties.

- Challenges
  - explicit geometry for transparent/specular objects still hard
  - unnatural multi-view capture, e.g. orbiting around the scene (cite); impractical for shelves, walls
  - long learning times

- RGBGrasp
  - multi-view grasping, high-resolution 3D target scenarios
  - eye-on-hand camera captures views as gripper approaches object; small disparities
  - goal: precise and fast reconstruction
  - monocular depth priors (pre-trained) + NeRF reconstruction for limited views
  - hash encoding + new sampling proposal network for speed

- Contributions
  - depth rank loss (cite) with trained depth estimator; sparse views; beats conventional NeRF with constrained angles
  - hash encoding + proposal sampler -> faster reconstruction
  - experiments: multi-view and sparse-view, grasping and perception; consistently better than recent approaches

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Robotic object grasping is a key challenge in robotics, because real-world objects have very diverse shapes and material properties. To do the task we need accurate estimation of the 3D geometry, especially for deciding the grasping pose afterwards. Point-cloud sensors are common in current approaches, but they have trouble with transparent and specular objects, so in these cases the 3D information about the environment that they capture is unreliable. Also, the point clouds from these sensors often have low resolution and suffer from problems like noise.

Because of these issues, there is growing interest in using the RGB modality to improve object grasping. One line of research tries to get 3D scene perception from a single image. For example, one work uses a single RGB image to estimate 3D object detection and pose, and another work uses a single image to predict 2D keypoints together with their depth information.

The reasoning behind single-image grasping models is simple, but inferring 3D geometry from just one image is inherently hard, mainly because there is no scale information. So current approaches mostly use multi-view RGB data to reconstruct the full 3D scene. For example, one method uses the neural radiance field (NeRF) framework to combine information from multiple viewpoints, and in this way gets precise grasping for objects with different material properties.

Current multi-view grasping algorithms have achieved impressive results, but they still face some challenges. First, it is still hard to accurately reconstruct explicit geometry for 3D scenes that contain objects with different material properties, such as transparent and specular objects. Second, these algorithms usually need an unnatural way of collecting multi-view data, for example the NeRF-based method above needs a series of frames captured by orbiting around the target scene. This is a problem for example when objects are on shelves or against walls, where it is impractical to capture images from some angles. Third, multi-view methods usually need long learning times, which limits how they can be used in real-world scenarios.

Because of the challenges of the earlier algorithms, we introduce RGBGrasp, a new multi-view grasping algorithm that aims to reconstruct high-resolution 3D target scenarios. In our setup an eye-on-hand camera captures multiple views of the scene while the gripper is approaching the object during manipulation. These views only have small disparities, but we want both precise scene reconstruction and fast reconstruction. More precisely, we combine prior geometric information from pre-trained monocular depth estimation networks with the 3D reconstruction ability of neural radiance fields, so that we can reconstruct the 3D scene precisely even with limited views. We also use hash encoding and a new sampling proposal network to make the learning for the target 3D scenarios faster. Our contributions are as follows:

- We introduce depth rank loss, with help from a trained depth estimation model, which allows precise geometric estimation when views are sparse. This gets around the limitations of conventional NeRF methods, especially in environments where the viewing angles are constrained.

- We combine a hash-encoding strategy with a proposal sampler strategy, which makes the 3D scenario reconstruction faster.

- We did experiments for both multi-view and sparse-view scenarios, including grasping and perception tasks. RGBGrasp consistently performed better than recent approaches.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Robotic object grasping is a pivotal challenge in robotics because of the diverse morphology and material properties of real-world objects. The task requires accurate 3D geometry estimation, particularly for determining the grasping pose afterwards. Although point-cloud sensors are prevalent in current approaches [1,2], they struggle with transparent and specular objects, which makes the captured 3D environmental information unreliable in these scenarios. In addition, point clouds from these sensors often suffer from low-resolution 3D observations and issues like noise [3].

In light of these considerations, there has been growing interest in leveraging the RGB modality to improve object grasping. One avenue of research focuses on achieving 3D scene perception from a single image. For instance, [4] uses a single RGB image to estimate 3D object detection and pose, while [5] uses a single image to predict 2D keypoints along with their corresponding depth information.

Despite the straightforward rationale behind single-image-based grasping models, inferring 3D geometric information from a single image is inherently challenging, notably due to the absence of scale information [6]. Consequently, contemporary approaches mainly harness multi-view RGB data to reconstruct complete 3D scenes. For instance, [7] leverages the neural radiance field (NeRF) [8] framework to aggregate information from multiple viewpoints, achieving precise grasping of items with diverse material properties.

Despite the impressive achievements of contemporary multi-view-based grasping algorithms, they still face persistent challenges. First, accurately reconstructing explicit geometric representations of 3D scenes that contain objects with varying material properties, such as transparent and specular objects, remains difficult. Second, these algorithms typically require an unnatural multi-view data collection process; for example, [7] requires a series of frames captured by orbiting around the target scene. This is impractical when objects are positioned on shelves or against walls, where images cannot be captured from certain angles. Third, multi-view-based methods typically involve long learning times, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios.

Given these challenges, we introduce RGBGrasp, a novel multi-view grasping algorithm aimed at reconstructing high-resolution 3D target scenarios. In our configuration, an eye-on-hand camera captures multiple views of the scene as the gripper approaches the object during manipulation. Although these views exhibit only minor disparities, we aim for both precise scene reconstruction and efficient reconstruction speed. Specifically, we integrate prior geometric information from pre-trained monocular depth estimation networks with the 3D reconstruction capabilities of neural radiance fields to achieve precise 3D scene reconstruction with limited views. We also use hash encoding and a novel sampling proposal network to speed up learning for the targeted 3D scenarios. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- • We introduce depth rank loss [9], aided by a trained depth estimation model, enabling precise geometric estimation under sparse views. This overcomes the limitations of conventional NeRF methods, particularly in environments with constrained viewing angles.

- • We integrate a hash-encoding strategy with a proposal sampler strategy, which accelerates 3D scenario reconstruction.

- • We conducted experiments in both multi-view and sparse-view scenarios, covering grasping and perception tasks. RGBGrasp consistently outperformed recent approaches.

References:
[1] A. Ten Pas, M. Gualtieri, K. Saenko, and R. Platt, “Grasp pose detection in point clouds,” The International Journal of Robotics Research , vol. 36, no. 13-14, pp. 1455–1473, 2017.
[2] H. Liang, X. Ma, S. Li, M. Görner, S. Tang, B. Fang, F. Sun, and J. Zhang, “Pointnetgpd: Detecting grasp configurations from point sets,” in 2019 International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) . IEEE, 2019, pp. 3629–3635.

[5] G. Zhai, D. Huang, S.-C. Wu, H. Jung, Y. Di, F. Manhardt, F. Tombari, N. Navab, and B. Busam, “Monograspnet: 6-dof grasping with a single rgb image,” in 2023 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) . IEEE, 2023, pp. 1708–1714.
